topic.title: Binary Search
topic.summary: Halve the search space every step: classic search, lower/upper bound, rotated arrays, 2D matrices and "binary search on the answer" — with templates that avoid off-by-one bugs.
topic.overview:
**Binary search** finds something in **O(log n)** by asking one yes/no question about the middle of a range and throwing away the half that cannot contain the answer. A million elements need about 20 steps; a billion need about 30.

It is not only for "find x in a sorted array". The real skill interviewers test is spotting a **monotonic condition** — something that is false, false, …, true, true (or the reverse) — and binary searching the boundary. That covers lower/upper bound, rotated arrays, the minimum speed / capacity / time that works ("binary search on the answer"), and square roots.

### What interviewers expect from a new grad
- Write the classic search **bug-free** on the first try, and explain the **loop invariant** (what `[lo, hi]` means) and why the loop terminates.
- Use the **overflow-safe midpoint** `lo + (hi − lo) / 2` and know why it matters in Java/C++.
- Know the **lower-bound** template (first index with `nums[i] ≥ target`) and when to use `lo < hi` + `hi = mid` versus `lo <= hi` + `hi = mid − 1`.
- Handle modified inputs: rotated arrays, duplicates, 2D matrices.
- Recognise "minimise the maximum / find the smallest value such that…" as **binary search on the answer**.

### How to study this topic
1. Memorise two templates — closed `[lo, hi]` for exact match, half-open `[lo, hi)` for the first true — and never mix their updates.
2. Before coding, say out loud: *what does the interval mean, what does the loop condition mean, and which side keeps `mid`?*
3. Test every solution mentally on 1- and 2-element arrays — that is where off-by-one bugs and infinite loops hide.

cheatsheet.title: Core facts
points: O(log n) time, O(1) space iteratively
Needs sorted data or a monotonic yes/no condition
Midpoint: lo + (hi − lo) / 2 — (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow int

cheatsheet.title: Template 1 — exact match, closed [lo, hi]
points: found → return mid; too small → lo = mid + 1; too big → hi = mid − 1
If not found, lo is the insertion position

cheatsheet.title: Template 2 — first true, half-open [lo, hi)
points: lo = 0, hi = n (n is a valid answer), while (lo < hi)
condition(mid) true → hi = mid; false → lo = mid + 1
Returns lo = first index where the condition holds (n if none)
Lower bound: nums[i] ≥ x · upper bound: nums[i] > x

cheatsheet.title: Binary search on the answer
points: Write feasible(k) and check it is monotonic
Minimum feasible k → template 2; maximum feasible k → mirror it or save ans
Cost = O(log range × cost of feasible)

cheatsheet.title: Off-by-one checklist
points: Does every branch shrink the range? (lo = mid with floor mid can loop forever)
Is the answer allowed to be n or −1?
Try arrays of length 1 and 2 before you say "done"
Rotated arrays: nums[lo] <= nums[mid] (with =) means the left half is sorted

patterns.name: Classic exact match (closed interval)
patterns.whenToUse: Sorted array with distinct values, find the index of a target or report −1.

patterns.name: Lower bound / first true (half-open)
patterns.whenToUse: First index where a monotonic condition becomes true: insert position, first occurrence, first bad version.

patterns.name: Binary search on the answer
patterns.whenToUse: "Minimum speed / capacity / days such that …" where checking one candidate is easy and feasibility is monotonic.

questions.title: Binary Search
questions.prompt:
You are given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers sorted in ascending order and an integer `target`.

Return the index of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if it does not occur. Your solution must run in **O(log n)** time.

examples.explanation: 4 would sit between 3 and 5, but it is not there.

constraints: All values are distinct and sorted ascending
hints: A linear scan ignores the fact that the array is sorted. What does one comparison with the middle element tell you?
If nums[mid] < target, can the target be at index mid or to its left?
Keep [lo, hi] as the range that could still contain the target; move lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid − 1 and stop when lo > hi.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Check every element until you find the target.

approaches.name: Iterative binary search
approaches.idea: Compare with the middle of [lo, hi] and discard the half that cannot contain the target.

solution.summary: Keep a search space [lo, hi] that must contain the target if it exists. Compare the middle element: if it is the target return it; if it is smaller move lo to mid + 1, otherwise move hi to mid − 1. When lo passes hi the target is absent. Each step halves the space, so it is O(log n).
solution.explanation:
**Loop invariant:** if `target` is in the array, its index is in `[lo, hi]`. Every update keeps this true:
- `nums[mid] < target` → because the array is sorted, indices `lo..mid` are all too small → `lo = mid + 1`.
- `nums[mid] > target` → indices `mid..hi` are all too big → `hi = mid − 1`.

**Termination:** each iteration removes at least `mid` itself, so the interval shrinks and the loop ends. When `lo > hi` the interval is empty and the target cannot exist.

**Overflow-safe mid:** in Java/C++ `(lo + hi) / 2` overflows when `lo + hi > 2³¹ − 1` (a real bug that sat in the JDK's own binary search for years). `lo + (hi − lo) / 2` gives the same value without overflow. JavaScript numbers are doubles (exact up to 2⁵³) and Python ints are unbounded, but writing the safe form is a good habit — and `(lo + hi) >> 1` in JavaScript breaks above 2³¹ because `>>` works on 32-bit integers.

**Why `<=`:** with a closed interval, `lo == hi` is still a one-element range that must be checked.

**Complexity:** the range halves each step, so at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 iterations — about 20 for a million elements, 30 for a billion.

complexity.time: O(log n) — the search space halves every iteration
complexity.space: O(1) — three integer variables (a recursive version uses O(log n) stack)

keyPoints: State the invariant: the target, if present, is always inside [lo, hi]
Closed interval → while (lo <= hi), lo = mid + 1, hi = mid − 1
Overflow-safe midpoint: lo + (hi − lo) / 2
Precondition: the data must be sorted (or the predicate monotonic)
When the loop ends without a match, lo is the insertion position

visuals.title: Finding target = 12
visuals.caption: Light-blue range = current search space [lo, hi], amber = mid being compared, red = the half being discarded, grey = already discarded.

steps.note: Start with the whole array as the search space: `lo = 0`, `hi = 7`. Invariant: **if `target` is in the array, it is inside [lo, hi]**.
`mid = 3`, `nums[mid] = 3 < 12`. The array is sorted, so everything at or left of mid is too small: `lo = mid + 1 = 4`.
`mid = 5`, `nums[mid] = 9 < 12`. The array is sorted, so everything at or left of mid is too small: `lo = mid + 1 = 6`.
`mid = 6 + ⌊(7 − 6) / 2⌋ = 6` and `nums[6] = 12` equals the target. Return **6**.

visuals.title: Target not present: target = 4
visuals.caption: The search space shrinks to nothing; lo ends at the insertion position.

steps.note: Start with the whole array as the search space: `lo = 0`, `hi = 7`. Invariant: **if `target` is in the array, it is inside [lo, hi]**.
`mid = 3`, `nums[mid] = 3 < 4`. The array is sorted, so everything at or left of mid is too small: `lo = mid + 1 = 4`.
`mid = 5`, `nums[mid] = 9 > 4`. Everything at or right of mid is too big: `hi = mid − 1 = 4`.
`mid = 4`, `nums[mid] = 5 > 4`. Everything at or right of mid is too big: `hi = mid − 1 = 3`.
Now `lo = 4 > hi = 3`: the search space is empty, so the loop stops and we return **-1**. Bonus: `lo` is exactly where 4 would be inserted.

visuals.title: Linear scan vs binary search (worst case comparisons)

pitfalls: Using while (lo < hi) with hi = mid − 1 — the last remaining element is never checked
Writing lo = mid or hi = mid in the closed template — the interval can stop shrinking and loop forever
(lo + hi) / 2 overflowing in Java/C++ for large indices
Running binary search on unsorted data

followUps.question: Recursive or iterative?
followUps.answer: Both are O(log n) time; the iterative version uses O(1) space while recursion uses O(log n) call-stack frames. Interviewers usually prefer iterative.

followUps.question: What if the array can contain duplicates and you need the first occurrence?
followUps.answer: When nums[mid] == target, record mid and keep searching left (hi = mid − 1) instead of returning — or use the lower-bound template.

followUps.question: What if the array size is unknown (an infinite sorted stream)?
followUps.answer: Exponential search: probe indices 1, 2, 4, 8, … until the value exceeds the target, then binary search inside the last window. Still O(log p) where p is the target position.

questions.title: Search Insert Position
questions.prompt:
Given a sorted array of **distinct** integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` if it exists. Otherwise return the index where it **would be inserted** to keep the array sorted.

Your algorithm must run in **O(log n)** time.

examples.explanation: Larger than everything → insert at the end (index = length).

constraints: nums is sorted ascending with distinct values
hints: Both cases (found / not found) have the same answer: the first index whose value is ≥ target.
The answer can be nums.length — so your search range must include that index.
Use a half-open range [lo, hi) with hi = nums.length. If nums[mid] < target move lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. Return lo.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Return the first index whose value is ≥ target, or n.

approaches.name: Classic binary search, return lo
approaches.idea: Run the closed-interval search; if the target is missing, lo ends at the insertion point. Works, but the reasoning is less obvious.

approaches.name: Lower-bound template
approaches.idea: Search for the first index with nums[i] ≥ target in [0, n) with lo < hi, hi = mid, lo = mid + 1.

solution.summary: This is a lower-bound search: find the first index whose value is ≥ target. I keep a half-open range [lo, hi) starting at [0, n); if nums[mid] < target the answer is right of mid (lo = mid + 1), otherwise mid might be the answer (hi = mid). When lo meets hi, that index is both the position of the target and its insertion point.
solution.explanation:
**Reframe:** "find the target or where it would go" = "find the **first index i with nums[i] ≥ target**" (or `n` if none). That is called the **lower bound** (C++ `std::lower_bound`, Python `bisect_left`, Java's `Arrays.binarySearch` returns `-(insertionPoint) - 1` when the key is missing, but with duplicates it may return *any* matching index, so it is not a guaranteed lower bound).

**The template**
1. `lo = 0`, `hi = n` — half-open `[lo, hi)`, so `n` itself is a possible answer.
2. While `lo < hi`: `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`.
   - `nums[mid] < target` → mid is not the answer and nothing left of it is → `lo = mid + 1`.
   - otherwise → mid satisfies the condition and might be the *first* one → `hi = mid` (keep it).
3. Return `lo` (`== hi`).

**Why it terminates:** `mid < hi` always (it rounds down), so `hi = mid` strictly shrinks the range, and `lo = mid + 1` strictly grows `lo`.

**Why this template matters:** the same 6 lines solve "first occurrence", "count of elements < x", "first bad version", and every "binary search on the answer" problem — only the condition changes.

complexity.time: O(log n) — the half-open range halves every iteration

keyPoints: Recognise it as lower bound: first index with nums[i] ≥ target
hi starts at n (not n − 1) because inserting at the end is valid
lo < hi, hi = mid, lo = mid + 1 — never hi = mid − 1 in this template
Mention bisect_left / std::lower_bound as the library equivalents

visuals.title: Lower bound of target = 12 in [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20]
visuals.caption: Light-blue range = [lo, hi), amber = mid. hi may point one past the end.

steps.note: Half-open search space `[lo, hi) = [0, 7)`. `hi` starts at `nums.length` because the target may belong **after** every element. Invariant: the answer is always in [lo, hi].
`mid = 3`, `nums[mid] = 11 < 12`: mid and everything left of it are too small, so `lo = mid + 1 = 4`.
`mid = 5`, `nums[mid] = 17 ≥ 12`: mid **could be** the answer, so keep it: `hi = mid = 5` (not mid − 1).
`mid = 4`, `nums[mid] = 14 ≥ 12`: mid **could be** the answer, so keep it: `hi = mid = 4` (not mid − 1).
`lo === hi === 4`: the range is empty and both point at the first element ≥ 12 (14). Insert 12 at index **4**.

visuals.title: Binary search finds the boundary between F and T
visuals.caption: The yes/no row "nums[i] ≥ target?" is always F…F T…T on sorted data; the answer is the first T.

steps.note: Rewrite the question as a yes/no test per index: "is nums[i] ≥ target?". Because nums is sorted, the answers look like F F … F T T … T. Binary search finds the **first T**. target = 12: the first T is index **4**: 12 goes between 11 and 14.
target = 8: the first T is index **2**, and nums[2] = 8 — the target itself.
target = 1: every element is ≥ 1, so the first T is index **0**.
target = 25: every element is smaller, so the boundary is at the end: **7** (= nums.length).

pitfalls: Starting with hi = n − 1, which makes "insert at the end" impossible to return
Writing hi = mid − 1 in the half-open template — it can skip the answer
Mixing templates: while (lo <= hi) with hi = mid can loop forever when lo == hi
Returning -1 when the target is missing instead of the insertion index

followUps.question: How would you find the last index with nums[i] ≤ target?
followUps.answer: Compute the upper bound (first index with nums[i] > target, condition nums[mid] <= target → lo = mid + 1) and subtract 1.

followUps.question: How do you count how many elements are smaller than x in a sorted array?
followUps.answer: It is exactly lowerBound(x): every index before the first element ≥ x holds a smaller value. O(log n).

questions.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
questions.prompt:
Given an array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order (it **may contain duplicates**) and a `target`, return `[first, last]`: the index of the first and the last occurrence of `target`. If `target` does not occur, return `[-1, -1]`.

Your algorithm must run in **O(log n)** time — even when the target appears many times.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Finding *one* copy is a normal binary search. Why is expanding left and right from it not O(log n)?
Run binary search twice: once biased to the left, once biased to the right.
When nums[mid] == target, save mid as a candidate and continue: hi = mid − 1 to find the first, lo = mid + 1 to find the last.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Walk the array and remember the first and last index equal to target.

approaches.name: Binary search + expand
approaches.idea: Find any copy, then walk left and right while values equal target. Degrades to O(n) when the array is mostly target.

approaches.name: Two biased binary searches
approaches.idea: On a match, record the index and keep searching left (first) or right (last). Equivalent: lowerBound(target) and lowerBound(target + 1) − 1.

solution.summary: Run binary search twice. In both runs, when nums[mid] equals the target I record mid as a candidate but do not stop: for the first position I continue left with hi = mid − 1, for the last position I continue right with lo = mid + 1. Each run is O(log n), so the whole thing is O(log n).
solution.explanation:
**Why not find one and expand?** If the array is `[5, 5, 5, …, 5]`, expanding touches every element — O(n). The requirement is O(log n) regardless of duplicates.

**Biased binary search**
1. Standard closed-interval loop with an extra `ans = -1`.
2. `nums[mid] < target` → `lo = mid + 1`; `nums[mid] > target` → `hi = mid − 1` (as usual).
3. `nums[mid] == target` → `ans = mid`, then:
   - searching for the **first**: `hi = mid − 1` (maybe there is an earlier copy),
   - searching for the **last**: `lo = mid + 1` (maybe there is a later copy).
4. When the loop ends, `ans` holds the extreme match (or -1).

**Why it is correct:** every match moves the boundary past `mid` toward the side we care about, and `ans` always holds the best match found so far. The loop only stops when no unexplored index on that side can still hold the target.

**Alternative with the lower-bound template:** `first = lowerBound(target)`; if `first == n` or `nums[first] != target` return `[-1, -1]`; `last = lowerBound(target + 1) − 1` (safe for 32-bit ints within the constraints) or use an `upperBound` with `<=`.
keyPoints: Explain why "find one and expand" is O(n) in the worst case
On a match, record and keep searching toward the boundary
One helper with an isFirst flag avoids duplicating the loop
Mention the lower bound / upper bound formulation (bisect_left / bisect_right)

visuals.title: Two biased searches for target = 5
visuals.caption: Green mid = a match that is recorded; the search continues toward the boundary. Light-blue range = [lo, hi].

steps.note: Search 1 (`isFirst = true`): a normal binary search, except that finding 5 does not stop it — we record `ans` and keep looking **left**.
`nums[4] = 5` — a match. Record `ans = 4`, but an earlier 5 may exist, so `hi = mid − 1 = 3`.
`nums[1] = 3 < 5`: every copy of 5 is to the right → `lo = 2`.
`nums[2] = 3 < 5`: every copy of 5 is to the right → `lo = 3`.
`nums[3] = 5` — a match. Record `ans = 3`, but an earlier 5 may exist, so `hi = mid − 1 = 2`.
`lo = 3 > hi = 2`, so search 1 ends. The last recorded match is the **first** position: 3.
Search 2 (`isFirst = false`): same loop from scratch, but after a match we keep looking **right**.
`nums[4] = 5` — a match. Record `ans = 4`, but a later 5 may exist, so `lo = mid + 1 = 5`.
`nums[6] = 5` — a match. Record `ans = 6`, but a later 5 may exist, so `lo = mid + 1 = 7`.
`nums[7] = 8 > 5`: every copy of 5 is to the left → `hi = 6`.
Search 2 ends with `ans = 6`. Answer: **[3, 6]** — two O(log n) searches, even if the whole array were 5s.

visuals.title: Find one + expand vs two binary searches
rows: Fast when the target is rare
One helper called twice with a flag

pitfalls: Returning as soon as nums[mid] == target — you get *a* copy, not the first or last
Expanding linearly from one match — O(n) when the target repeats a lot
Not handling the empty array (hi = −1, the loop simply does not run — make sure you return [-1, -1])
Using target + 1 with Integer.MAX_VALUE in Java (overflow) — use an upper-bound search instead

followUps.question: How many times does target occur?
followUps.answer: last − first + 1 when found (or upperBound − lowerBound), still O(log n).

followUps.question: Python one-liner?
followUps.answer: lo = bisect_left(nums, t); hi = bisect_right(nums, t) − 1; return [lo, hi] if lo <= hi else [-1, -1].

questions.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.prompt:
An array of **distinct** integers was sorted in ascending order and then **rotated** at an unknown index: for example `[2, 5, 9, 12, 15, 18, 22]` may become `[15, 18, 22, 2, 5, 9, 12]`.

Given the rotated array `nums` and a `target`, return the index of `target` or `-1` if it is not present, in **O(log n)** time.
constraints: nums is an ascending array rotated by some amount (possibly 0)
hints: Split the array at mid. Is it possible that *neither* half is sorted?
Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid] to find out which half is sorted.
If the target lies within the value range of the sorted half, search there; otherwise search the other half.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Check every element.

approaches.name: Find the rotation point, then binary search
approaches.idea: Binary search for the minimum (rotation index), decide which sorted run can contain the target, then run a classic binary search on it.

approaches.name: One-pass modified binary search
approaches.idea: At each mid, one half is sorted. Check whether the target is inside that sorted half's range and discard the other half accordingly.

solution.summary: Use binary search, but at each step first find which half is sorted: if nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] the left half is sorted, otherwise the right half is. If the target falls inside the sorted half's range I search there, otherwise I search the other half. Each step still halves the range, so it is O(log n).
solution.explanation:
**Key fact:** cutting a rotated sorted array at any `mid` gives two halves, and **at least one of them is fully sorted** — the rotation point can only be in one of them.

**Steps**
1. Classic loop `while (lo <= hi)`, return `mid` on a match.
2. If `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` → **left half sorted**. The target is in it iff `nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]` → `hi = mid − 1`; else `lo = mid + 1`.
3. Otherwise → **right half sorted**. The target is in it iff `nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]` → `lo = mid + 1`; else `hi = mid − 1`.

**Why `<=` in `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`:** when `lo == mid` (two elements left) the "left half" is the single element `nums[lo]`, which is trivially sorted. Using `<` would wrongly treat it as unsorted.

**Why only one sorted half is enough:** in a sorted range, "is the target inside?" is a simple bounds check. If it is not inside, it can only be in the other half — so we always discard half the array.

**Duplicates (follow-up):** with duplicates, `nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi]` gives no information; shrink with `lo++` / `hi--`, which makes the worst case O(n).

complexity.time: O(log n) — one half is discarded every iteration

keyPoints: At any mid, at least one half is sorted
nums[lo] <= nums[mid] identifies the sorted half (note the <=)
Range check only on the sorted half; otherwise go to the other half
Duplicates break the guarantee → worst case O(n)

visuals.title: Searching target = 5 in [18, 22, 27, 30, 2, 5, 9, 12, 15]
visuals.caption: Green range = the half that is sorted at this step, red = the half being discarded, light blue = search space.

steps.note: The array was sorted, then rotated. At any `mid`, **at least one half is still sorted** — and in a sorted half one range check tells us if `target = 5` can be there.
`nums[lo] = 18 > nums[mid] = 2`: the rotation point is in the left half, so the **right half [4..8] is sorted**. 5 is in (2, 15], so search there: `lo = 5`.
`nums[lo] = 5 ≤ nums[mid] = 9`, so the **left half [5..6] is sorted**. 5 is in [5, 9), so it can only be there: `hi = 5`.
`nums[5] = 5` is the target. Return **5**.

visuals.title: Why one half is always sorted
visuals.caption: The rotated array is two ascending runs; mid lands in one of them. Grey = outside [lo, hi].

steps.note: A rotated sorted array is **two sorted runs**: [18, 22, 27, 30] and [2, 5, 9, 12, 15]. Every value in run 1 is bigger than every value in run 2.
Suppose `lo = 0`, `hi = 4`, so `mid = 2` lands in run 1: `nums[lo] = 18 ≤ nums[mid] = 27`, so **[lo..mid] is sorted** (green). The drop 30 → 2 must be in the other half.

Suppose `lo = 2`, `hi = 8`, so `mid = 5` lands in run 2: `nums[lo] = 27 > nums[mid] = 5`, so the drop is on the left and **[mid..hi] is sorted** (green). Either way one half is sorted, and a range check on it decides where to go.

The boundary between the runs (index 4, value 2) is the **minimum** and equals the number of rotations. You never need to find it for this problem, but *Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array* locates it with the same idea in O(log n).

pitfalls: Using nums[lo] < nums[mid] (strict) — fails when lo == mid, e.g. nums = [3, 1], target = 1
Wrong inclusive/exclusive bounds in the range check (target < nums[mid] vs <=)
Checking the unsorted half's range — the min/max of that half are not at its ends
Claiming O(log n) when the array can contain duplicates

followUps.question: What if the array contains duplicates?
followUps.answer: When nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] you cannot tell which half is sorted, so shrink both ends (lo++, hi--). Average is still fast, but the worst case becomes O(n), e.g. [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1].

followUps.question: How do you find the rotation count?
followUps.answer: It equals the index of the minimum element — see Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (O(log n)).

questions.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.prompt:
An ascending array of **distinct** integers has been rotated by an unknown amount (possibly 0), e.g. `[2, 5, 7, 11, 13]` → `[11, 13, 2, 5, 7]`.

Return the **minimum** element in **O(log n)** time.

examples.explanation: Rotated 0 times — the array is fully sorted.

hints: The minimum is the only element smaller than the one before it — the "drop".
Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. What does nums[mid] > nums[hi] tell you about where the drop is?
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the minimum is in (mid, hi] → lo = mid + 1. Otherwise it is in [lo, mid] → hi = mid. Stop when lo == hi.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Return the smallest element (or the first element smaller than its predecessor).

approaches.name: Binary search comparing with nums[hi]
approaches.idea: If nums[mid] > nums[hi] the drop is to the right of mid; otherwise [mid..hi] is sorted and the minimum is at mid or to its left.

solution.summary: Binary search for the drop by comparing nums[mid] with nums[hi]: if nums[mid] is bigger, the minimum is strictly to the right, so lo = mid + 1; otherwise mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or to its left, so hi = mid. When lo meets hi, that element is the minimum.
solution.explanation:
**Picture:** a rotated array climbs, drops once, and climbs again. The minimum is the bottom of the drop.

**Compare with `nums[hi]`**
- `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` → going from mid to hi the values must go down at some point → the drop (minimum) is in `(mid, hi]` → `lo = mid + 1`.
- `nums[mid] < nums[hi]` → `[mid..hi]` is increasing → nothing right of mid is smaller → the minimum is in `[lo, mid]` → `hi = mid` (mid itself may be the minimum, so keep it).

Loop while `lo < hi`; the range always contains the minimum and shrinks every iteration (`mid < hi`), so it ends with `lo == hi` on the minimum.

**Why not compare with `nums[lo]`?** For a non-rotated array `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]`, `nums[mid] > nums[lo]` would suggest "go right", which is wrong — the minimum is at index 0. Comparing with `hi` handles the 0-rotation case without a special check.

**Bonus:** the index of the minimum is the number of rotations, and it splits the array into the two sorted runs used by *Search in Rotated Sorted Array*.

complexity.time: O(log n) — the range [lo, hi] halves every iteration

keyPoints: Minimum = the bottom of the single "drop"
Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi], not nums[lo]
hi = mid (not mid − 1) because mid may be the minimum; loop while lo < hi
Works for 0 rotations without a special case
Duplicates: when nums[mid] == nums[hi], do hi-- (worst case O(n))

visuals.title: Finding the drop in [11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 2, 5, 7]
visuals.caption: Light-blue range = [lo, hi] (always contains the minimum), amber = mid, red = the part being discarded.

steps.note: The minimum is where the values drop (19 → 2). Keep `[lo, hi]` so that it always contains the minimum, and compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]`.
`nums[mid] = 17 > nums[hi] = 7`: values go *down* somewhere between mid and hi, so the minimum is **right of mid** → `lo = 4`.
`nums[mid] = 2 ≤ nums[hi] = 7`: [mid..hi] is sorted, so nothing right of mid can be smaller than nums[mid]. The minimum is mid or left of it → `hi = mid = 5` (keep mid).
`nums[mid] = 19 > nums[hi] = 2`: values go *down* somewhere between mid and hi, so the minimum is **right of mid** → `lo = 5`.
`lo === hi === 5`: only one candidate is left — the minimum is **2** (index 5, which is also the number of rotations).

visuals.title: Edge case: not rotated at all — [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
visuals.caption: Comparing with nums[hi] correctly walks hi down to index 0.

steps.note: No rotation: the array is already sorted, so the answer is index 0. A version that compares with `nums[lo]` would be tempted to go right here.
`nums[mid] = 6 ≤ nums[hi] = 10`: [mid..hi] is sorted, so nothing right of mid can be smaller than nums[mid]. The minimum is mid or left of it → `hi = mid = 2` (keep mid).
`nums[mid] = 4 ≤ nums[hi] = 6`: [mid..hi] is sorted, so nothing right of mid can be smaller than nums[mid]. The minimum is mid or left of it → `hi = mid = 1` (keep mid).
`nums[mid] = 2 ≤ nums[hi] = 4`: [mid..hi] is sorted, so nothing right of mid can be smaller than nums[mid]. The minimum is mid or left of it → `hi = mid = 0` (keep mid).
`lo === hi === 0`: only one candidate is left — the minimum is **2** (index 0, which is also the number of rotations).

pitfalls: Comparing with nums[lo] — breaks on an array that was not rotated
Writing hi = mid − 1 — can skip the minimum when mid is the minimum
Using while (lo <= hi) with hi = mid — infinite loop when lo == hi
Returning lo (the index) when the question asks for the value, or vice versa

followUps.question: What if duplicates are allowed?
followUps.answer: If nums[mid] == nums[hi] you cannot tell which side the drop is on. Dropping hi (hi--) is still safe: even if nums[hi] is a minimum, nums[mid] has the same value and stays in range. Worst case O(n), e.g. [1, 1, 1, 0, 1].

followUps.question: How many times was the array rotated?
followUps.answer: The index of the minimum (lo at the end).

questions.title: Koko Eating Bananas
questions.prompt:
Koko has `piles` of bananas, where `piles[i]` is the number of bananas in pile `i`, and `h` hours before the guards return (`h ≥ piles.length`).

She picks an integer eating speed `k` (bananas per hour). Each hour she chooses one pile and eats `k` bananas from it; if the pile has fewer than `k`, she finishes it and **does not start another pile that hour**.

Return the **minimum** integer `k` that lets her finish every pile within `h` hours.

examples.explanation: At k = 4 the piles take 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours. At k = 3 they take 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9 hours — too slow.
Only 5 hours for 5 piles: each pile must be finished in one hour, so k must be the biggest pile.
At k = 23 only the pile of 25 needs 2 hours (6 in total). At k = 22 the pile of 23 needs 2 hours as well (7 in total).

hints: If speed k works, does speed k + 1 also work?
The answer lies between 1 and max(piles). Checking one candidate speed costs O(n).
Binary search over k: if hoursNeeded(k) ≤ h, the answer is k or smaller (hi = k); otherwise it is larger (lo = k + 1).

approaches.name: Try every speed
approaches.idea: For k = 1, 2, 3, … return the first k with hoursNeeded(k) ≤ h.

approaches.name: Binary search on the answer
approaches.idea: Feasibility is monotonic in k, so binary search the smallest feasible k in [1, max(piles)], computing hours in O(n) per check.

solution.summary: Binary search on the answer: the speed is between 1 and max(piles), and if a speed is fast enough then every faster speed is too. For a candidate mid I compute the hours as the sum of ceil(pile / mid); if it fits in h I try slower (hi = mid), otherwise faster (lo = mid + 1). That is O(n log max).
solution.explanation:
**Recognise the pattern:** the question asks for the *minimum value that satisfies a condition*, and the condition is **monotonic** — if Koko can finish at speed `k`, she can finish at any `k' > k`. Whenever a yes/no check looks like `F F F T T T` over the possible answers, you can binary search the boundary.

**Steps**
1. Search space: `lo = 1`, `hi = max(piles)` (at that speed every pile takes exactly one hour, and `h ≥ piles.length`).
2. Feasibility check `hoursNeeded(k) = Σ ceil(p / k)` — O(n).
3. Lower-bound loop: `while (lo < hi)`: if feasible, `hi = mid` (mid might be the answer); else `lo = mid + 1`.
4. Return `lo`.

**Integer ceil:** in Java and Python use `(p + k − 1) / k` with integer division (`//` in Python). JavaScript only has floating-point division; `Math.ceil(p / k)` is exact here because every value is far below 2⁵³.

**Overflow:** with 10⁴ piles of 10⁹ bananas and k = 1 the total is 10¹³ hours — use `long` in Java (JavaScript numbers are exact up to 2⁵³, Python ints are unbounded).

**Same template, other problems:** capacity to ship packages within D days, split array largest sum, minimum days to make bouquets, aggressive cows — only the feasibility function changes.

complexity.time: O(n log M) — log M binary-search steps (M = max pile), each summing n piles

keyPoints: Binary search the answer space [1, max(piles)], not the array
Monotonic feasibility: if k works, every larger k works
Lower-bound template: feasible → hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1
Integer ceil (p + k − 1) / k and long for the hour sum in Java
Name other problems with the same template

visuals.title: Binary search over speeds for piles = [3, 6, 7, 9], h = 8
visuals.caption: Top row: candidate speeds with lo/mid/hi. Bottom row: hours each pile takes at speed mid (green = fits in h, red = too slow).

steps.note: We are not searching the piles — we search the **answer**: speeds 1…9. Speed 9 (the biggest pile) always works because each pile then takes one hour, and 4 piles ≤ h = 8.
Try `mid = 5`: hours = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = **7 ≤ 8**. Speed 5 is fast enough, but a slower one might be too → `hi = mid = 5`.
Try `mid = 3`: hours = 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = **9 > 8**. Too slow — and every slower speed is even slower → `lo = mid + 1 = 4`.
Try `mid = 4`: hours = 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = **8 ≤ 8**. Speed 4 is fast enough, but a slower one might be too → `hi = mid = 4`.
`lo === hi === 4`: the smallest speed that finishes in time is **4** (1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours). Only 3 feasibility checks instead of trying all 9 speeds.

visuals.title: Why binary search applies: the feasibility row is monotonic
visuals.caption: hours(k) only goes down as k grows, so "hours(k) ≤ h" flips from false to true exactly once.

steps.note: Hours needed for every possible speed. As k grows, the hours **never increase** — that monotonic shape is what makes binary search legal.
Compare each value with h = 8. Speeds 1…3 need more than 8 hours (red) — **too slow**. Notice they form a prefix: once a speed is fast enough, it stays fast enough.
Every speed from 4 up is feasible (green). The yes/no row reads **F F F T T T T T T** — exactly one boundary, the same shape as "nums[i] ≥ target" on a sorted array.
The answer is the **first feasible speed**: k = 4. Binary search finds this boundary in O(log max) checks, exactly like lower bound on a sorted array.

pitfalls: Searching from 0 (division by zero) — the smallest speed is 1
Forgetting the ceil: integer p / k rounds down. In Java, Math.ceil(p / k) on two ints is still wrong because the int division happens before ceil runs
int overflow of the total hours in Java when k is small
Using hi = mid − 1 when mid is feasible — it may skip the minimum

followUps.question: How do you recognise "binary search on the answer" problems?
followUps.answer: The question asks for a minimum (or maximum) value such that some condition holds, the answer range is large (often up to 10⁹), and you can check a single candidate quickly. If the check is monotonic, binary search it.

followUps.question: Can you tighten the lower bound?
followUps.answer: Yes: k ≥ ceil(sum(piles) / h), because she can eat at most k·h bananas. It does not change the big-O but saves a few iterations.

questions.title: Search a 2D Matrix
questions.prompt:
You are given an `m × n` integer matrix with two properties:

1. each row is sorted in ascending order, and
2. the first value of every row is greater than the last value of the previous row.

Return `true` if `target` is in the matrix, otherwise `false`, in **O(log(m · n))** time.
hints: Read the matrix row by row. What do you get?
A flat index k in [0, m·n) corresponds to row k / n and column k % n.
Run a classic binary search over flat indices and convert mid to (row, col) to read the value.

approaches.name: Scan every cell
approaches.idea: Check all m · n values.

approaches.name: Staircase from the top-right
approaches.idea: Move left when the value is too big, down when it is too small. Also works for matrices sorted only by row and column.

approaches.name: Two binary searches
approaches.idea: Binary search the row whose range contains the target, then binary search inside that row.

approaches.name: One binary search on the flattened index
approaches.idea: Treat the matrix as a sorted array of length m · n and map mid → (mid / n, mid % n).

solution.summary: Because every row starts after the previous row ends, the matrix read row by row is one sorted array of m·n values. I run a normal binary search over indices 0 to m·n − 1 and convert each mid to row = mid / n and column = mid % n — O(log(m·n)) with O(1) space and no copying.
solution.explanation:
**Observation:** properties 1 and 2 together mean the row-major order `matrix[0][0], matrix[0][1], …, matrix[m−1][n−1]` is sorted.

**Index mapping (no copy needed):** a flat index `k` lives at `row = ⌊k / n⌋`, `col = k % n` (`n` = number of columns). Example: in a 3 × 4 matrix, k = 9 → row 2, col 1.

**Algorithm:** classic closed-interval binary search on `[0, m·n − 1]`, reading `matrix[mid / n][mid % n]` instead of `nums[mid]`.

**Note:** `log(m·n) = log m + log n`, so this has the same complexity as "find the row, then search inside it" — the flattened version is just less code.

**Different matrix (Search a 2D Matrix II):** if rows and columns are sorted independently (row starts do *not* continue the previous row), flattening is wrong. Use the **staircase** search from the top-right corner: O(m + n).

complexity.time: O(log(m · n)) — binary search over m · n cells
complexity.space: O(1) — index arithmetic instead of copying the matrix

keyPoints: Row-major order of this matrix is sorted → one binary search
mid → (mid / cols, mid % cols); divide by the number of COLUMNS
No need to build a flattened copy
Know the staircase O(m + n) alternative and when it is required

visuals.title: Binary search on flat indices, target = 29
visuals.caption: Light blue = cells still in [lo, hi], amber = mid cell being compared, grey = discarded.

steps.note: Each row continues where the previous one ended, so reading row by row gives one sorted list of 12 values. Search flat indices `lo = 0` … `hi = 11`.
`mid = 5` → row 5 / 4 = 1, col 5 % 4 = 1: value 15 < 29 → `lo = 6` (discard this cell and everything before it).
`mid = 8` → row 8 / 4 = 2, col 8 % 4 = 0: value 25 < 29 → `lo = 9` (discard this cell and everything before it).
`mid = 10` → row 10 / 4 = 2, col 10 % 4 = 2: value 33 > 29 → `hi = 9` (discard this cell and everything after it).
`mid = 9` → row 9 / 4 = 2, col 9 % 4 = 1: value 29 equals the target. Return **true**.

visuals.title: Alternative: staircase search from the top-right corner
visuals.caption: Grey = rows / columns already ruled out, light blue = cells that can still hold the target, amber = the corner being compared. Each comparison removes one row or one column — O(m + n).

steps.note: Alternative: start at the **top-right** corner. Everything left of it in the row is smaller, everything below it in the column is bigger — so each comparison removes a whole row or column. Light blue = cells that can still hold the target.
9 < 29: this is the largest value left in row 0, so the whole row is too small → move **down** (row 0 turns grey).
21 < 29: this is the largest value left in row 1, so the whole row is too small → move **down** (row 1 turns grey).
40 > 29: this is the smallest value left in column 3, so the whole column is too big → move **left** (column 3 turns grey).
33 > 29: this is the smallest value left in column 2, so the whole column is too big → move **left** (column 2 turns grey).
29 equals the target — found after 5 comparisons. Staircase search is O(rows + cols) and also works when only rows and columns are sorted separately.

pitfalls: Dividing by the number of rows instead of columns when mapping mid → (row, col)
Copying the matrix into a new array first (O(m · n) time and space)
Applying the flattened search to a matrix where only rows and columns are sorted separately
Forgetting an empty matrix check if the constraints allow m = 0 or n = 0

followUps.question: What if each row and each column is sorted, but a row does not start after the previous row ends?
followUps.answer: Flattening no longer gives a sorted array. Use staircase search from the top-right (or bottom-left) corner: O(m + n).

followUps.question: Could rows * cols overflow?
followUps.answer: Not with 100 × 100, but for huge virtual grids compute it in a long (Java) before using it as hi.

questions.title: Sqrt(x) — integer square root
questions.prompt:
Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the **integer square root** of `x`: the square root rounded **down** to the nearest integer (i.e. the largest `k` with `k² ≤ x`).

You may not use built-in exponent or square-root functions such as `Math.sqrt`, `pow` or `x ** 0.5`.
hints: The answer is an integer between 0 and x. Can you check a single candidate quickly?
If k² ≤ x then every smaller k also satisfies it — the condition is monotonic.
Binary search k in [0, x]: when mid² ≤ x save mid and go right, otherwise go left. Watch out for mid² overflowing.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Increase k from 0 while (k + 1)² ≤ x.

approaches.name: Binary search on the answer
approaches.idea: Search the largest k in [0, x] with k² ≤ x, keeping the best valid mid.

approaches.name: Newton's method
approaches.idea: Iterate r = (r + x / r) / 2 starting from r = x until r² ≤ x. Converges quadratically, but is harder to prove correct in an interview.
approaches.time: O(log x) iterations, very fast in practice

solution.summary: Binary search on the answer: the square root is between 0 and x, and "mid² ≤ x" is true for a prefix of candidates. If mid² ≤ x, I store mid as the best answer so far and search right; otherwise I search left. In Java I compute mid² as a long to avoid overflow. O(log x).
solution.explanation:
**Reframe:** find the **largest** integer `k` with `k² ≤ x`. The predicate `k² ≤ x` is true for 0, 1, …, ⌊√x⌋ and false afterwards — a monotonic T…T F…F pattern, so binary search applies.

**Steps**
1. `lo = 0`, `hi = x`, `ans = 0`.
2. While `lo <= hi`: `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`.
   - `mid * mid <= x` → `ans = mid`, `lo = mid + 1` (try bigger).
   - otherwise → `hi = mid − 1`.
3. Return `ans`.

**Overflow:** for x near 2³¹ − 1, `mid` can be ~10⁹ and `mid * mid` ~10¹⁸ overflows a 32-bit int. In Java cast to `long` (or compare `mid <= x / mid` for mid > 0). In JavaScript the product is a double; it is inexact only when it is far larger than x, so the comparison is still right. Python ints never overflow.

**Small optimisation:** for x ≥ 2 the root is at most x / 2, so `hi = x / 2` saves one iteration — not required.

**The "save the best answer" pattern** (record `ans` and keep searching) is the closed-interval way to write "last true"; the half-open lower-bound template works too.

complexity.time: O(log x) — at most 31 iterations for x ≤ 2³¹ − 1

keyPoints: Turn it into "largest k with k² ≤ x" — binary search on the answer
Keep the last valid mid in ans while moving right
mid * mid overflows int in Java → use long or mid <= x / mid
Edge cases: x = 0 and x = 1

visuals.title: Binary search for the integer square root of 9
visuals.caption: Top row: candidate answers k with lo/mid/hi. Bottom row: k² — green squares fit (≤ 9), grey do not.

steps.note: We want the **largest k with k² ≤ 9**. Candidates are 0…9, and "k² ≤ 9" is true for a prefix of them (green below) — so binary search the last true.
`mid = 4`, 4² = 16 > 9: too big, and so is everything above it → `hi = 3`.
`mid = 1`, 1² = 1 ≤ 9: 1 is a valid answer. Save `ans = 1` and look for a bigger one: `lo = 2`.
`mid = 2`, 2² = 4 ≤ 9: 2 is a valid answer. Save `ans = 2` and look for a bigger one: `lo = 3`.
`mid = 3`, 3² = 9 ≤ 9: 3 is a valid answer. Save `ans = 3` and look for a bigger one: `lo = 4`.
`lo = 4 > hi = 3`, the loop ends. The last value that fitted is **3** (3² = 9 ≤ 9 < 16 = 4²).

visuals.title: Three ways to compute ⌊√x⌋ for x = 2³¹ − 1
rows: Halve [0, x] on the test mid² ≤ x
r = (r + x / r) / 2 until r² ≤ x
O(log x), quadratic convergence near the root

pitfalls: mid * mid overflowing a 32-bit int in Java (or C++)
Returning lo instead of the saved ans (lo ends one past the answer)
Starting with lo = 1 and forgetting x = 0
Using floating point sqrt and rounding errors for large x

followUps.question: How would you compute the square root to 5 decimal places?
followUps.answer: Binary search on doubles: loop a fixed number of times (e.g. 60) or until hi − lo < 1e-6, moving lo or hi based on mid * mid ≤ x. Or use Newton's method.

followUps.question: How do you check if a number is a perfect square?
followUps.answer: Compute k = mySqrt(x) and check k * k == x. O(log x).

questions.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
questions.prompt:
Given two arrays `a` and `b`, each sorted in ascending order (sizes `m` and `n`, not both empty), return the **median** of all `m + n` values combined.

- Odd total: the middle value. Even total: the average of the two middle values.
- Target complexity: **O(log(min(m, n)))** — better than merging.
hints: Merging gives O(m + n). The median only needs to know which values form the smaller half.
If you take i elements from a for the left half, how many must come from b?
Binary search i in the shorter array. The cut is valid when a[i−1] ≤ b[j] and b[j−1] ≤ a[i]; if a[i−1] > b[j], move left, else move right.

approaches.name: Merge then pick
approaches.idea: Merge both arrays (two pointers) and read the middle element(s).

approaches.name: Two pointers without storing
approaches.idea: Walk the merge only up to the middle, remembering the last two values.

approaches.name: Binary search the partition
approaches.idea: Choose how many of the left-half elements come from the shorter array; the cut is valid when both cross-comparisons hold.

solution.summary: I do not need to merge — I only need to split all values into a left half and a right half where every left value is ≤ every right value. If I take i elements from the shorter array, I must take half − i from the other, so I binary search i: if a[i−1] > b[j] I took too many from a, if b[j−1] > a[i] too few. At a valid cut the median comes from max(left) and min(right). O(log min(m, n)).
solution.explanation:
**Reframe the median:** it only depends on the boundary between the smaller half and the larger half of the combined values.

**Partition idea:** let `half = ⌊(m + n + 1) / 2⌋` be the size of the left half (the extra element goes left when the total is odd). Taking the first `i` elements of `a` and the first `j = half − i` elements of `b` forms a left half of the right size. It is the **correct** left half iff
- `a[i − 1] ≤ b[j]` and
- `b[j − 1] ≤ a[i]`

(each array is already sorted internally, so only the cross pairs need checking). Missing neighbours at the ends count as −∞ / +∞.

**Binary search on i in [0, m]:**
- `a[i − 1] > b[j]` → too many from `a` → `hi = i − 1`.
- `b[j − 1] > a[i]` → too few from `a` → `lo = i + 1`.
- valid → odd total: `max(aLeft, bLeft)`; even total: `(max(aLeft, bLeft) + min(aRight, bRight)) / 2`.

**Why search the shorter array:** it keeps `j = half − i` inside `[0, n]` for every `i` in `[0, m]` and gives O(log min(m, n)).

**In the interview:** start with the O(m + n) merge (it is a perfectly good first answer), then explain the partition idea. Getting the sentinels and the odd/even case right matters more than speed.

complexity.time: O(log min(m, n)) — binary search over cut positions in the shorter array

keyPoints: Median = boundary between the left half and the right half
i from a forces j = half − i from b; search only i
Valid cut: aLeft ≤ bRight and bLeft ≤ aRight (−∞/+∞ at the ends)
Search the shorter array so j stays in range
Odd: max(left); even: (max(left) + min(right)) / 2

visuals.title: Binary search on the cut: a = [1, 5, 9, 27, 28], b = [7, 13, 14, 17, 24]
visuals.caption: Light-blue ranges = elements in the left half. i and j point at the first element of each right part; red = the pair that violates the cut, green = the values that give the median.

steps.note: Merged, the 10 values split into a **left half of 5** and a right half. Taking `i` elements from `a` forces `j = 5 − i` from `b`, so we only binary search **i in [0, 5]**.
i = 2, j = 3: bLeft = 14 > aRight = 9 — b gave too much to the left half, so we took **too few from a** → `lo = i + 1 = 3`.
i = 4, j = 1: aLeft = 27 > bRight = 13 — a value on the left is bigger than one on the right, so we took **too many from a** → `hi = i − 1 = 3`.

i = 3, j = 2: aLeft 9 ≤ bRight 14 and bLeft 13 ≤ aRight 27 — a **valid cut**: every left value ≤ every right value. Even total, so the median is (max(left) + min(right)) / 2 = (13 + 14) / 2 = **13.5**.

visuals.title: Merge vs partition binary search
rows: Merge until the middle, read the middle value(s)
Find i, j so that every left value ≤ every right value
O(1) if you only walk to the middle
Off-by-one in the sentinels and the odd/even case

pitfalls: Binary searching the longer array — j = half − i can go negative or past n
Forgetting the −∞ / +∞ sentinels when i or j is 0 or at the end
Using half = (m + n) / 2 but then taking max(left) as the median for odd totals (the middle element ends up on the right)
Integer division when averaging the two middle values in Java (cast to double)

followUps.question: How would you find the k-th smallest element of two sorted arrays?
followUps.answer: Same partition idea with half replaced by k, or the recursive version that discards k/2 elements from one array per step: O(log k).

followUps.question: What if the data arrives as a stream?
followUps.answer: Then binary search does not apply; keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half (O(log n) insert, O(1) median).

quiz.question: About how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case on 1,000,000 sorted elements?
quiz.explanation: Each comparison halves the range: 2²⁰ ≈ 1,048,576, so about 20 steps. 500,000 is the average for a linear scan.

quiz.question: Why do Java and C++ programmers write `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2`?
options: It rounds up instead of down
It avoids int overflow when lo + hi exceeds 2³¹ − 1
It is required for half-open intervals
quiz.explanation: For large arrays lo + hi can exceed the int range and become negative. hi − lo never overflows, and the result is the same midpoint (still rounded down).

quiz.question: Binary search over an array only works if the array is…
options: sorted (or the condition you test is monotonic)
quiz.explanation: Discarding half the range is only safe when one comparison tells you which side the answer is on — that requires sorted order or a monotonic condition. Length and sign do not matter, and a linked list has no O(1) access to the middle.

quiz.question: The classic `while (lo <= hi)` search for target 4 in [1, 3, 5, 7] fails. What is lo when the loop ends?
quiz.explanation: mid = 1 (3 < 4) → lo = 2; mid = 2 (5 > 4) → hi = 1; loop ends with lo = 2 — exactly where 4 would be inserted.

quiz.question: This loop can run forever. What is the fix?
quiz.explanation: When hi = lo + 1, mid rounds down to lo, so `lo = mid` makes no progress. nums[mid] < target means mid cannot be the answer, so lo = mid + 1 is both correct and guarantees progress. Rounding up would just move the infinite loop to the `hi = mid` branch.

quiz.question: What does this print?

code.code:
import bisect
a = [1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 7]
print(bisect.bisect_left(a, 4), bisect.bisect_right(a, 4))

quiz.explanation: bisect_left returns the first index with a[i] ≥ 4 (index 2). bisect_right returns the first index with a[i] > 4 (index 5, the 7). The 4s occupy [2, 5).

quiz.question: In Search in Rotated Sorted Array, which check proves that the left half [lo..mid] is sorted?
quiz.explanation: If the rotation point were inside [lo..mid], nums[lo] would be larger than nums[mid]. The = matters when lo == mid. nums[mid] > nums[hi] tells you the RIGHT half contains the drop.

quiz.question: In Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, why compare nums[mid] with nums[hi] rather than nums[lo]?
options: Comparing with nums[lo] goes the wrong way when the array is not rotated at all
nums[lo] might be out of bounds
quiz.explanation: For [2, 4, 6, 8, 10], nums[mid] > nums[lo] would push the search right, away from the minimum at index 0. nums[mid] ≤ nums[hi] correctly says "[mid..hi] is sorted, go left".

quiz.question: Why can Koko Eating Bananas be solved with binary search?
options: h is always a power of two
If speed k finishes in time, every faster speed does too
quiz.explanation: Feasibility is monotonic in k (F F F T T T over speeds), so we can binary search the first feasible speed. The piles do not need to be sorted.

quiz.question: A 3 × 4 matrix (3 rows, 4 columns) is searched as a flat sorted array. Which cell is flat index 7?
quiz.explanation: row = 7 / cols = 7 / 4 = 1, col = 7 % 4 = 3. Dividing by the number of rows (3) instead would give the wrong answer row 2, col 1.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of Koko Eating Bananas with n piles and maximum pile size M?
quiz.explanation: Binary search over speeds 1…M takes O(log M) iterations, and each feasibility check sums all n piles.

quiz.question: In JavaScript, why is `const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1` risky for very large ranges?
options: `>>` converts to a signed 32-bit integer, so sums ≥ 2³¹ become wrong (negative)
It rounds up instead of down
It is much slower than Math.floor
It only works when lo + hi is even
quiz.explanation: Bitwise operators work on signed 32-bit integers. While lo + hi < 2³¹ it rounds down like Math.floor, but for binary search on large answer ranges (e.g. up to 2 · 10⁹) use lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2).
